scope.start: 10b: the baraita on a get placed in her courtyard and the dispute between R. Yannai and Abba Kohen Bardela (11a opens mid-exchange)
scope.end: 11b: Rav Ashi begins his distinction between a gift and a get (continues on 12a)

sections.title: Chatzer as Yad: Get Only, or Metziah Too? Three Readings
sections.gist: All agree that a *chatzer* acts as her *yad* for a *get*. The Gemara then locates the dispute between R. Yannai and Abba Kohen Bardela three ways: *get* vs. *metziah*, girl vs. boy, or no dispute at all.

bullets.text: Challenge: does anyone deny that a *chatzer* works as a *yad*? A baraita derives from "*ve'natan be'yadah*" that a *get* placed on her roof, in her *chatzer* or in her *karpef* divorces her.
The derivation rests on the word *yad*, and the verb "and he gives" extends it to any place she holds. So for a *get*, the *chatzer* is an extension of her hand.
Answer: for a *get* everyone agrees that a *chatzer* counts as her *yad*. The dispute is over a *metziah* found in her *chatzer*.

children.title: First Reading: Do We Learn Metziah from Get?
children.gist: R. Yannai learns *metziah* from *get*; Abba Kohen Bardela does not.

bullets.text: R. Yannai: we derive *metziah* from *get*, so her *chatzer* acquires a found object for her as her *yad*.
Abba Kohen Bardela: we don't derive *metziah* from *get*.
Why distinguish at all? A *get* may need only to be placed on her person, not acquired. *Metziah* requires real *kinyan*, and "placement" in her domain may not be enough for that.

children.title: Second Reading: Katan Learned from Ketanah?
children.gist: All agree that a *ketanah* acquires a *metziah* through her *chatzer*; the dispute is whether a *katan* does too.

bullets.text: For a minor girl, all learn *metziah* from *get*: she acquires an ownerless item in her *chatzer*.
R. Yannai: a *katan* is learned from a *ketanah*; there is no difference between them in *kinyan*.
Abba Kohen Bardela: only a *ketanah* acquires by *chatzer*, since the Torah included it for her through *get*.

children.title: Third Reading: No Dispute, Two Separate Statements
children.gist: Abba Kohen Bardela spoke of a minor girl's *get* and R. Yannai of a minor's *metziah*; they don't disagree.

bullets.text: Abba Kohen Bardela: a *ketanah* is divorced by a *get* placed in her *chatzer*.
R. Yannai: a minor boy or girl does not acquire a *metziah* in his or her *chatzer*.

This is surprising. Once the Torah shows that a *chatzer* can serve as a *yad*, why should the rule differ between domains? It makes sense only if *yad* means something different for a *get* than for acquisition.
Open question: a *katan* cannot acquire a *metziah* by Torah law for lack of *da'at*. Where someone actively gives to the minor (*da'at acheret*), his *chatzer* should presumably work.

sections.title: Mishnah: 'Zakhtah Li Sadi': Crippled Deer and Fledglings vs. Runners and Fliers
sections.gist: A field acquires an animal crossing it only if the animal can't easily escape: a deer with a broken leg or chicks that can't yet fly, not a healthy deer or flying birds.

bullets.text: People are chasing a deer with a broken leg or young pigeons that can't fly. The field owner says "my field has acquired it for me", and he acquires it.
If the deer runs normally or the pigeons fly, his statement is meaningless: a *chatzer* can't acquire an item that won't stay in it.
*Kinyan chatzer* depends on containment. The field must actually be able to hold the object.

sections.title: Omed Be'Tzad Sadehu: Why a Field Needs Its Owner Beside It
sections.gist: Shmuel requires the owner to stand beside his field; the Gemara explains this by *chatzer she'einah mishtameret*, proves it from *shikhechah*, and cites Ulla and Rabbah bar bar Chana in agreement.

children.title: Shmuel's Condition vs. R. Yosei b. R. Chanina: Mishtameret or Not
children.gist: A *chatzer* acquires without the owner's knowledge only when it is secured; an unsecured field acquires only while he stands beside it.

bullets.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: the Mishnah's *kinyan* works only when the owner is standing beside his field.
Difficulty: R. Yosei son of R. Chanina says a person's *chatzer* acquires for him even without his knowledge.
Answer: that is a *chatzer ha'mishtameret*. An unsecured *chatzer* acquires only if the owner stands beside it.
The owner's presence does for an open field what a fence does for a yard: it makes the field *mishtameret*.
Tosafot: the Mishnah's spoken declaration isn't strictly required, since a *chatzer* acquires even without *da'at*.

children.title: Proof from Shikhechah: Forgotten in the Field vs. in the Town
children.gist: A baraita on the forgotten sheaf shows that the owner's field holds a remembered sheaf for him only while he is in the field. The Gemara defends the reading against a "Torah edict" alternative, and Rav Ashi grounds it in "it shall be".

children.title: The Baraita's Contradiction and Its Reading
children.gist: The baraita seems to say both that a sheaf forgotten from town is *shikhechah* and that it isn't; the Gemara reads it as distinguishing remembered-then-forgotten sheaves by where the owner stands.

bullets.text: Baraita: the owner in town says "I know my workers forgot a sheaf; since I remember it, it won't be *shikhechah*." Then he forgets it too. One might think it isn't *shikhechah*, so the verse teaches... "in the field" and not in the town.
The baraita contradicts itself: its first clause seeks to make it *shikhechah*, while "not in the town" seems to exempt it.

Reading: in the field, a sheaf forgotten from the outset is *shikhechah*, but one remembered and later forgotten is not, because his field is his *chatzer* and acquires it for him once he remembers it.
In town, even a remembered-then-forgotten sheaf is *shikhechah*, since he isn't beside his field. So a *chatzer* acquires only when the owner stands beside it.

A striking explanation: one might have expected the reason to be the owner's supervision and memory. The Gemara makes it a formal matter of possession: his presence means he never lost hold of the sheaf.
Consequence: an owner who steps twenty feet away at the moment the workers forget it, while still remembering the sheaf, loses it to *shikhechah*.

children.title: Torah Edict? 'Lo Tashuv', Pe'ah 7:4, and Rav Ashi's 'Yihyeh'
children.gist: Perhaps the town/field rule is a bare decree; the Gemara looks for a verse including the town case, rejects "do not go back" as needed elsewhere, and Rav Ashi finds it in "it shall be".

bullets.text: Rejection: perhaps it is simply a Torah decree that *shikhechah* applies in the field and not in town, unrelated to *kinyan*.
Response: "you shall not go back to take it" includes sheaves forgotten in town, so town and field don't differ in *shikhechah* itself.
Challenge: that phrase is needed to prohibit taking the forgotten sheaf. Answer: then "you shall not take it" would suffice; "go back" is extra.
Challenge: "go back" is needed for Pe'ah 7:4: a sheaf still ahead of him isn't *shikhechah*, and one already behind him is.
Rav Ashi: the town case is included by "it shall be". So the original reading stands, and Shmuel's rule is confirmed.

children.title: Ulla and Rabbah bar bar Chana Concur
children.gist: Two more amora'im state the same requirement of standing beside the field.

bullets.text: Ulla and Rabbah bar bar Chana also say the Mishnah's *kinyan* works only when the owner stands beside his field.

sections.title: Rabban Gamliel's Tithes on the Ship: Chatzer, Agav or Da'at Acheret?
sections.gist: R. Abba challenges Ulla from Rabban Gamliel giving tithes from a ship. The answers: *agav* rather than *chatzer* (debated through *chalifin* and *tovat hana'ah*), and Rav Pappa's *da'at acheret*, tested against Ulla's ruling on a *get*.

children.title: The Challenge and Ulla's Dismissal
children.gist: R. Yehoshua and R. Akiva acquired tithes through rented places in Rabban Gamliel's field while they were all on a ship, far from it; Ulla brushes the question aside.

bullets.text: Ma'aser Sheni 5:9: on a ship, Rabban Gamliel gives the tithe he will measure out to Yehoshua ben Chananya the Levite, "and its place is rented to him". He gives the poor man's tithe to Akiva ben Yosef, to acquire for the poor, and rents him its place too.
R. Abba: were R. Yehoshua and R. Akiva standing beside Rabban Gamliel's field? They were all on the ship.
Ulla: he seems like one who hasn't learned *halakha*. The Gemara takes this as a dismissal, not an answer.
Rashi and Tosafot differ on the scene: separating tithes from afar lest his household eat *tevel*, or transferring tithes already separated.
Tosafot also asks whether the field was *mishtameret* at all, even from his own household.

children.title: In Sura: Agav, Not Chatzer? Chalifin and Tovat Hana'ah
children.gist: A Sage in Sura says the tithes went *agav* the rented land. Rava objects that *chalifin* would have been simpler, so he must have owned only *tovat hana'ah*; the Gemara answers that tithes require giving, and *agav* is giving while *chalifin* is sale.

bullets.text: A Sage in Sura: Rabban Gamliel transferred the movables *agav* the land, not through a *chatzer*. R. Zeira accepted this; R. Abba did not.
*Agav*: acquiring land carries along the movables bundled with it, wherever they are. So there is no need to stand beside the field.

Rava: R. Abba was right. If Rabban Gamliel owned the tithes, a cloth for *chalifin* would have done. So he owned only *tovat hana'ah*, which is not property, and can't pass by *agav* either. It must have been *chatzer*.
Rejection: tithes must be *given* (Devarim 26:12). *Chalifin* is a form of buying and selling, while movables *agav* land is a powerful form of giving. So it was *agav*, and Ulla stands.

chart.caption: Why Rabban Gamliel used rented land and not a cloth
rows: Had he owned the tithes, a cloth would have sufficed
*Agav* the land, a form of giving
*Chalifin* is sale; tithes must be given

children.title: Rav Pappa: Da'at Acheret Makneh, and the Get Objection
children.gist: Even through a *chatzer*, a gift from another mind needs no standing beside it, as R. Abba bar Kahana's ruling on gifted animals shows. The Gemara presses: why then does Ulla require it for a *get*? Rav Pappa's answer is refuted *kal va'chomer*, and Rav Ashi begins a new distinction.

bullets.text: Rav Pappa: when *da'at acheret makneh*, another mind transferring ownership, the *chatzer* acquires even without the recipient beside it.
Support: R. Yochanan limits the Mishnah to where he could run and catch the animals. R. Abba bar Kahana rules that a gift is acquired even when he couldn't, because another mind is giving.
Every *kinyan* joins *da'at* with a physical act. Where the giver's *da'at* is strong, a weaker act suffices.

Rav Shimi: yet Ulla says a *get* thrown into her house or *chatzer* works only if she stands beside it, though the husband gives it. Rav Pappa: a *get* differs, since it can be given against her will.
Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi: *kal va'chomer*: if a *get*, valid against her will, needs her beside it, a gift, received only willingly, should need it all the more.
Rav Ashi begins a different distinction between gift and *get*.

children.continues: Continues on 12a: Rav Ashi: a *chatzer* is a *yad* but no less than a *shaliach*, so it can benefit a person in his absence (a gift) but not act against him (a *get*).

key_terms.definition: A person's courtyard or land acquires movable objects that enter or are placed in it on his behalf, as if he had taken them himself.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The daf asks whether a minor's *chatzer* acquires, when an unsecured field acquires, and whether Rabban Gamliel's tithes passed through a *chatzer* at all.

key_terms.definition: One's hand as a means of acquisition; property treated as an extension of the person's hand acquires just as the hand does.
key_terms.on_this_daf: All agree that a *chatzer* counts as a woman's *yad* for a *get*; the dispute is whether that extends to *metziah* and to a minor boy.

key_terms.definition: A domain that guards what is in it without the owner's supervision, as opposed to open land from which items can easily be removed.
key_terms.on_this_daf: A secured courtyard acquires without the owner's knowledge; an unsecured field acquires only when he is standing beside it.

key_terms.definition: The requirement that the owner be present next to an unsecured field for the field to acquire for him.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Shmuel, Ulla and Rabbah bar bar Chana require it; it is proven from *shikhechah* and tested against Rabban Gamliel's tithes.

key_terms.sense: the forgotten sheaf left for the poor
key_terms.definition: A sheaf forgotten in the field during the harvest must be left for the poor, and the owner may not go back to take it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: A sheaf remembered and then forgotten is *shikhechah* only if the owner is in town, which proves that a field acquires only when its owner stands beside it.

key_terms.definition: When land is transferred, movable property can be transferred together with it by the same act, even if the movables are not located on that land.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Sura Sage's explanation of Rabban Gamliel's rental; the Gemara calls it a powerful form of giving.

key_terms.sense: the owner's right to choose who receives his gifts
key_terms.definition: The benefit a person has in choosing which kohen, Levite or poor person receives the gifts he must give; it is not considered ownership of the gifts.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rava argues that since Rabban Gamliel had only *tovat hana'ah*, he couldn't transfer the tithes by *chalifin* or *agav*.

key_terms.definition: An acquisition in which an owner actively transfers the item, as opposed to taking ownerless property; such transfers can succeed with a weaker act of acquisition.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Pappa's answer: a gift through a *chatzer* needs no standing beside it, tested against Ulla's rule for a *get*.

judgment_calls: The 10b opening (baraita on get and the 'everyone agrees' answer) is folded into s1 as its parent bullets, with the three readings as children, rather than outlined as a separate section.
The shikhechah proof is split into the baraita's reading (s9) and the verse-based defense (s10); these could be one section, but the verse debate is a distinct back-and-forth.
The Rav Shimi/Rav Sheshet get objection is kept inside Rav Pappa's section, since it tests his answer, rather than being made a separate section.
The earlier ein shaliach le'dvar aveirah material (10b) falls outside this daf's scope and was not outlined.
coverage_notes: The shiur's first two segments (chatzer as shaliach, ein shaliach le'dvar aveirah, the kohen and the rounding of the corners of the head, Tosafot and the Noda Biyehuda) cover 10b and are outside scope.

The essay says the baraita on shikhechah rules that the declaration from town is ineffective and that the owner in the field who remembers prevents shikhechah; the text says the case is where the owner remembered, then forgot, and it reads the baraita as the Gemara does. Followed the text, including the Torah-edict objection and Rav Ashi's 'it shall be', which the essay omits.
The essay attributes the challenge to Rav Abba; the text has R. Abba. Followed the text.

The essay presents Rava's objection as leading to agav's rejection and then says Rabban Gamliel used chatzer; the text has the Gemara reject Rava: agav is giving and chalifin is sale, so it was agav. Followed the text.
The essay says the owner's field is 'at best' secured and cites the sheaf as re-acquired; kept only as shiur framing.
Rav Shimi's get objection, Rav Sheshet's kal va'chomer and Rav Ashi's opening are not in the essay; outlined from the text within s15.
The essay calls the tithes 'ma'aser ani' for Akiva, consistent with the text; the source is Ma'aser Sheni 5:9 per the text.
